content: 1. Rifapentine should not be used as a once-weekly continuation phase regimen in combination with isoniazid for HIV-positive patients with pulmonary tuberculosis. This is due to an increased risk of treatment failure and/or relapse, often associated with the emergence of rifampin-resistant organisms. Additionally, rifapentine has not been studied as part of the initial phase treatment regimen in HIV-positive patients with pulmonary tuberculosis. 2. Rifapentine is an inducer of CYP450 enzymes. When used concurrently with drugs metabolized by these enzymes, such as protease inhibitors and reverse transcriptase inhibitors, it may significantly reduce their plasma concentrations, potentially leading to a loss of therapeutic efficacy. 3. Rifapentine should be used cautiously in patients with cavitary pulmonary lesions, positive sputum cultures after the initial treatment phase, or bilateral pulmonary disease, as these conditions are associated with higher relapse rates. Poor adherence to the prescribed dosage regimen, particularly during the initial phase of treatment with companion antituberculosis drugs, is linked to delayed sputum conversion and increased relapse rates. Emphasis must be placed on completing the full course of therapy and avoiding missed doses. HIV-positive patients receiving rifapentine during the continuation phase also exhibit higher relapse rates, with risk factors including baseline pulmonary and extrapulmonary disease, low CD4 counts, use of azole antifungals, and younger age. 4. Antituberculosis multidrug regimens, including rifapentine and other rifamycin-class drugs, are associated with serious hepatic events. Patients with abnormal liver function tests or liver disease should only receive rifapentine when absolutely necessary, under strict medical supervision. Liver function tests, particularly serum transaminases, should be monitored carefully before starting therapy and every 2 to 4 weeks during treatment. If signs of liver disease develop or worsen, rifapentine should be discontinued. The hepatotoxicity of other antituberculosis drugs, such as isoniazid and pyrazinamide, used in combination with rifapentine, should also be considered. 5. Hyperbilirubinemia may occur due to competition between rifapentine and bilirubin for excretory pathways, similar to the competition observed with rifampin. A moderate rise in bilirubin and/or transaminase levels does not automatically warrant discontinuation of treatment. Instead, repeat testing should be performed, and trends in these levels should be evaluated in conjunction with the patient’s clinical condition. 6. Rifapentine may cause a red-orange discoloration of body tissues and fluids, including the skin, teeth, tongue, urine, feces, saliva, sputum, tears, sweat, and cerebrospinal fluid. Contact lenses or dentures may become permanently stained. 7. Rifapentine should not be used in patients with porphyria. Rifampin, a related drug, has enzyme-inducing properties, including the induction of delta-aminolevulinic acid synthetase, which has been associated with porphyria exacerbation. Based on isolated reports of rifampin-induced porphyria exacerbation, rifapentine is presumed to have a similar effect. 8. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including rifamycins, and can range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, as it can occur up to two months after antibiotic administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate management includes fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation as clinically indicated.
